This manual follows **Steps 1–6 of Supplement S2.4, “Computation of the
MEC-Cox Estimator via the Dual Newton Solver,”** in the same order and with
the same notation. Each formula is followed by the R code that implements it.
The example uses the package's simulated data, logistic regression for source
propensity, Cox regression for control survival, and the Kullback–Leibler (KL)
generator. The general generator notation from the supplement is retained.

[R Markdown source](https://github.com/yain22/mecCox/blob/main/docs/mec-cox-implementation.Rmd)
· [Package repository](https://github.com/yain22/mecCox)

## Data and notation

The source indicator is $A_i=1$ for the treated cohort and $A_i=0$ for external
controls. Write $\mathcal I_a=\{i:A_i=a\}$ and $n_a=|\mathcal I_a|$.
The observed follow-up time and event indicator are stored in `time` and
`event`. The baseline covariates $X_i$ are `age`, `sex`, and `marker`.

| Supplement notation | R object | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $A_i$; $\mathcal I_0,\mathcal I_1$ | `A`; `I0`, `I1` | Source indicator and cohort row indices |
| $K$; $\kappa(i)$ | `K`; `kappa` | Number of folds and each subject's fold |
| $t_1,\ldots,t_L$, $L=p-1$ | `t_landmark`; `L`, `p` | Landmark times and number of calibration features |
| $\widehat h_i$ | row `i` of `H` | Intercept and held-out control-survival predictions |
| $\widehat\pi_i,\widehat q_i,\widehat d_i$ | `pi_hat`, `q_hat`, `d_hat` | Propensity, odds, and normalized baseline control weights |
| $H_0,H_1,T_H$ | `H0`, `H1`, `T_H` | Cohort-specific feature matrices and target totals |
| $\lambda,F(\lambda),J(\lambda)$ | `lambda`, `F`, `J` | Dual parameter, calibration residual, and Jacobian |
| $\widehat w_i,\widetilde\omega_i$ | `w_hat`, `omega_tilde` | Calibrated control weights and final weights for all subjects |

```{r data}
library(mecCox)
library(survival)
data(example_external_controls)
dat <- example_external_controls

A <- dat$source
I0 <- which(A == 0L)
I1 <- which(A == 1L)
n <- nrow(dat)
n0 <- length(I0)
n1 <- length(I1)
dat$A <- A
X_names <- c("age", "sex", "marker")

K <- 5L
seed <- 2026L
t_landmark <- c(3, 6, 9, 12, 15)
L <- length(t_landmark)
p <- L + 1L

data.frame(treated = n1, external_controls = n0,
           folds = K, landmarks = L, calibration_features = p)
```

Run the code chunks in order. The five landmark times are fixed for this
example; the same times and folds will be used in the package comparison.

## Step 1. Construction of the cross-fitted predictor basis

Partition the pooled sample into $K$ folds, stratified by $A_i$, and let
$\kappa(i)$ identify the fold containing subject $i$. For each fold $k$, train
the control-survival learner using only $\mathcal I_0\cap\mathcal J^{(-k)}$,
then predict survival for **all** subjects in the held-out fold $\mathcal J^{(k)}$.
The calibration-feature vector is

\[
\widehat h_i=
\left(1,\widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i))}(t_1\mid X_i),\ldots,
\widehat S_0^{(-\kappa(i))}(t_{p-1}\mid X_i)\right)\in\mathbb R^p.
\]

For the Cox survival learner used here,

\[
\widehat S_{0,\mathrm{Cox}}^{(-k)}(t_\ell\mid X_i)=
\exp\left[-\widehat\Lambda_{00}^{(-k)}(t_\ell)
\exp\{X_i^\top\widehat\beta_0^{(-k)}\}\right].
\]

```{r predictor-basis}
set.seed(seed)
kappa <- integer(n)
for (a in c(0L, 1L)) {
  rows <- which(A == a)
  kappa[rows] <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = length(rows)))
}

S0_hat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n, ncol = L)
survival_formula <- reformulate(X_names, response = "Surv(time, event)")

for (k in seq_len(K)) {
  train0 <- which(kappa != k & A == 0L)
  valid <- which(kappa == k)

  outcome_fit <- coxph(
    survival_formula, data = dat[train0, ],
    ties = "breslow", x = TRUE, singular.ok = FALSE,
    control = coxph.control(timefix = FALSE)
  )

  # Evaluate the baseline cumulative hazard at each landmark.
  baseline <- basehaz(outcome_fit, centered = FALSE)
  j <- findInterval(t_landmark, baseline$time)
  Lambda00_hat <- numeric(L)
  Lambda00_hat[j > 0L] <- baseline$hazard[j[j > 0L]]

  # Uncentered linear predictors match the uncentered baseline hazard.
  lp <- predict(outcome_fit, newdata = dat[valid, ],
                type = "lp", reference = "zero")
  S0_hat[valid, ] <- exp(-outer(exp(lp), Lambda00_hat))
}

colnames(S0_hat) <- paste0("S0(t=", t_landmark, ")")
H <- cbind(intercept = 1, S0_hat)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(H)), all(S0_hat >= 0 & S0_hat <= 1))
head(H, 3)
```

Each row is predicted without using that subject to train the survival model.
These predictions enter the calibration features; the final Cox model in Step 6
uses the source indicator $A_i$ as its sole regression covariate.

## Step 2. Baseline ATT odds weights

Using the same folds, fit the source propensity model on the **pooled training
sample** $\mathcal J^{(-k)}$. Evaluate it on $\mathcal J^{(k)}$ to obtain
$\widehat\pi_i=\widehat\pi^{(-k)}(X_i)$.
For $i\in\mathcal I_0$, form

\[
\widehat q_i=\frac{\widehat\pi_i}{1-\widehat\pi_i},
\qquad
\widehat d_i=\frac{n_1\widehat q_i}
{\sum_{j\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat q_j},
\qquad
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0}\widehat d_i=n_1.
\]

```{r baseline-weights}
pi_hat <- numeric(n)
propensity_formula <- reformulate(X_names, response = "A")

for (k in seq_len(K)) {
  train <- which(kappa != k)
  valid <- which(kappa == k)
  propensity_fit <- glm(propensity_formula, data = dat[train, ],
                        family = binomial())
  stopifnot(isTRUE(propensity_fit$converged))
  pi_hat[valid] <- predict(propensity_fit, newdata = dat[valid, ],
                           type = "response")
}

ps_trim <- c(0.01, 0.99)
pi_hat <- pmin(pmax(pi_hat, ps_trim[1]), ps_trim[2])
q_hat <- pi_hat[I0] / (1 - pi_hat[I0])
d_hat <- n1 * q_hat / sum(q_hat)

stopifnot(all(is.finite(d_hat)), all(d_hat > 0))
c(baseline_weight_total = sum(d_hat), treated_count = n1)
```

The truncation bounds are explicit so that the hand calculation and the package
use the same propensity scores. `d_hat` contains external-control weights only,
in the order specified by `I0`.

## Step 3. Formulation of the primal problem

Stack the rows $\widehat h_i$ within each cohort to obtain
$H_0\in\mathbb R^{n_0\times p}$ and $H_1\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times p}$.
The target calibration total is

\[
T_H=H_1^\top\mathbf 1_{n_1}
=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_1}\widehat h_i\in\mathbb R^p.
\]

The primal problem is

\[
\widehat w=\arg\min_{\{w_i>0:i\in\mathcal I_0\}}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0}D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad H_0^\top w=T_H,
\]

where $D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i)=G(w_i)-G(\widehat d_i)
-g(\widehat d_i)(w_i-\widehat d_i)$, $G$ is strictly convex, and $g=G'$.
The intercept constraint preserves the total external-control weight $n_1$;
the other constraints match the treated cohort's predicted-survival totals.

```{r primal-problem}
H0 <- H[I0, , drop = FALSE]
H1 <- H[I1, , drop = FALSE]
T_H <- colSums(H1)

# KL generator from the manuscript: G(u) = u log(u), for u > 0.
G <- function(u) u * log(u)
g <- function(u) 1 + log(u)
g_inv <- function(v) exp(v - 1)
g_prime <- function(u) 1 / u

data.frame(feature = colnames(H),
           treated_total = T_H,
           baseline_control_total = as.numeric(crossprod(H0, d_hat)),
           row.names = NULL)
```

We form this problem explicitly, then solve its $p$-dimensional dual instead of
optimizing over $n_0$ weights.

## Step 4. Conversion to the dual problem

Use the same Lagrangian sign as the supplement:

\[
\mathcal L(w,\lambda)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_0}D_G(w_i\|\widehat d_i)
-\lambda^\top(H_0^\top w-T_H).
\]

Stationarity gives $g(w_i)=g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i$, hence

\[
w_i(\lambda)=g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i\},
\qquad F(\lambda)=H_0^\top w(\lambda)-T_H=0.
\]

This is the dual estimating equation. For the KL choice above,
$g(u)=1+\log u$ and $g^{-1}(v)=\exp(v-1)$, so
$w_i(\lambda)=\widehat d_i\exp(\lambda^\top\widehat h_i)$.

```{r dual-problem}
w_of_lambda <- function(lambda) {
  nu <- g(d_hat) + as.numeric(H0 %*% lambda)
  g_inv(nu)
}

F <- function(lambda) {
  as.numeric(crossprod(H0, w_of_lambda(lambda)) - T_H)
}

lambda0 <- numeric(p)
stopifnot(max(abs(w_of_lambda(lambda0) - d_hat)) < 1e-12)
```

## Step 5. Dual Newton solver

Define $\nu_i(\lambda)=g(\widehat d_i)+\lambda^\top\widehat h_i$.
The dual domain contains values of $\lambda$ for which every
$\nu_i(\lambda)$ belongs to $\operatorname{dom}(g^{-1})$.
The Jacobian and Newton update are

\[
J(\lambda)=H_0^\top\operatorname{diag}
\left[\frac{1}{g'\{w_i(\lambda)\}}:i\in\mathcal I_0\right]H_0,
\]
\[
\{J(\lambda_m)+\rho I_p\}\Delta_m=F(\lambda_m),
\qquad \lambda_{m+1}=\lambda_m-\alpha_m\Delta_m.
\]

For KL, $1/g'(w_i)=w_i$. The code uses the supplement's choices
$\rho=10^{-8}$, $\varepsilon=10^{-10}$, and at most 100 Newton updates.
Each update starts with $\alpha_m=1$. KL has
$\operatorname{dom}(g^{-1})=\mathbb R$; the step-halving guard below also
rejects weights that overflow or underflow in finite-precision arithmetic.
Convergence requires $\|F(\widehat\lambda)\|_2\le\varepsilon$.

```{r newton-solver}
J <- function(lambda) {
  w <- w_of_lambda(lambda)
  crossprod(H0, H0 * (1 / g_prime(w)))
}

rho <- 1e-8
epsilon <- 1e-10
max_iter <- 100L
lambda <- lambda0
converged <- FALSE
history <- data.frame(iteration = integer(), residual_L2 = numeric())

for (m in 0:max_iter) {
  residual <- F(lambda)
  residual_L2 <- sqrt(sum(residual^2))
  history <- rbind(history, data.frame(iteration = m,
                                      residual_L2 = residual_L2))
  if (is.finite(residual_L2) && residual_L2 <= epsilon) {
    converged <- TRUE
    break
  }
  if (m == max_iter) break

  Delta <- solve(J(lambda) + rho * diag(p), residual)
  alpha <- 1
  accepted <- FALSE
  for (halving in 0:60) {
    candidate <- lambda - alpha * Delta
    w_candidate <- w_of_lambda(candidate)
    if (all(is.finite(w_candidate)) && all(w_candidate > 0)) {
      accepted <- TRUE
      break
    }
    alpha <- alpha / 2
  }
  if (!accepted) stop("No admissible Newton step was found.")
  lambda <- candidate
}

if (!converged) stop("The dual solver did not reach the stated tolerance.")
lambda_hat <- lambda
w_hat <- w_of_lambda(lambda_hat)
history
```

The balance table makes the constraint $H_0^\top\widehat w=T_H$ visible.

```{r calibration-check}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  feature = colnames(H),
  treated_mean = T_H / n1,
  baseline_control_mean = as.numeric(crossprod(H0, d_hat)) / n1,
  calibrated_control_mean = as.numeric(crossprod(H0, w_hat)) / n1
), digits = 6, row.names = FALSE,
col.names = c("Feature", "Treated mean", "Baseline control mean",
              "Calibrated control mean"))
```

## Step 6. Final MEC-Cox estimator

Recover $\widehat w_i=g^{-1}\{g(\widehat d_i)+\widehat\lambda^\top\widehat h_i\}$
for external controls. The final estimating-equation weights are

\[
\widetilde\omega_i=A_i+(1-A_i)\widehat w_i.
\]

Treated subjects retain weight one. Using these weights, define

\[
S_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}^{(r)}(t;\theta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\widetilde\omega_i\mathcal Y_i(t)
\exp(\theta A_i)A_i^r,\qquad r=0,1,
\]
\[
\overline A_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}(t;\theta)
=\frac{S_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}^{(1)}(t;\theta)}
{S_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}^{(0)}(t;\theta)}.
\]

Here $\mathcal Y_i(t)$ is the at-risk indicator and $\mathcal N_i(t)$ is the
event counting process. Solve

\[
U_n^{\mathrm{MEC}}(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\int\widetilde\omega_i
\{A_i-\overline A_{\mathrm{MEC},\omega}(t;\theta)\}\,d\mathcal N_i(t)=0
\]

and report $\widehat{\mathrm{HR}}_{\mathrm{MEC}}=\exp(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MEC}})$.
In R, the point estimate is obtained by fitting a weighted Cox model with
`A` as its sole covariate. Breslow handling of tied events matches the package.

```{r final-estimator}
omega_tilde <- rep(1, n)
omega_tilde[I0] <- w_hat
dat$omega_tilde <- omega_tilde

final_fit <- coxph(
  Surv(time, event) ~ A, data = dat, weights = omega_tilde,
  ties = "breslow", robust = FALSE,
  control = coxph.control(timefix = FALSE)
)
theta_hat <- unname(coef(final_fit)["A"])
HR_hat <- exp(theta_hat)
data.frame(log_hazard_ratio = theta_hat, hazard_ratio = HR_hat)
```

This step illustrates the point estimator. For the MEC stacked-sandwich
standard error and confidence interval, use `fit_mec_cox()` as below; the
ordinary weighted `coxph()` standard error is not that variance estimator.

## Agreement with `fit_mec_cox()`

The package call performs these calculations together. We supply the same
learners, folds, landmark times, and propensity bounds used above.

```{r package-comparison}
mec <- fit_mec_cox(
  example_external_controls,
  time = "time", event = "event", source = "source",
  covariates = X_names, ps_learner = "glm", survival_learner = "cox",
  n_folds = K, landmarks = t_landmark, seed = seed, ps_trim = ps_trim
)

# First verify the ingredients, before comparing the calibrated estimates.
stopifnot(
  identical(kappa, mec$fold_id),
  max(abs(pi_hat - mec$ps_oof)) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(H - mec$basis)) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(d_hat - mec$baseline_weights[I0])) < 1e-12
)

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  calculation = c("Steps 1-6", "fit_mec_cox()"),
  log_hazard_ratio = c(theta_hat, mec$theta),
  hazard_ratio = c(HR_hat, mec$hr),
  control_weight_total = c(sum(w_hat), sum(mec$weights[I0])),
  max_mean_balance_residual = format(
    c(max(abs(F(lambda_hat))) / n1,
      mec$calibration$max_mean_balance_residual), scientific = TRUE, digits = 3
  )
), digits = 6,
col.names = c("Calculation", "Log HR", "HR", "Control weight total",
              "Max. mean residual"))

stopifnot(max(abs(w_hat - mec$weights[I0])) < 1e-5,
          abs(theta_hat - mec$theta) < 1e-7)
```

The worked solver uses S2.4's numerical choices. The package solves the same
KL balance equation using a scaled ridge, a dual-objective line search, and
`calibration_tol` applied to $\max|F|/n_1$ (default $10^{-8}$). Accordingly,
the comparison checks numerical agreement rather than identical iterations.
The public `fit_mec_cox()` implementation uses KL calibration; the supplement's
general $G$ notation also describes other generators.

For routine analysis, the package also returns the MEC uncertainty estimates:

```{r uncertainty}
data.frame(hazard_ratio = mec$hr, SE_log_hazard_ratio = mec$se,
           CI_lower = unname(mec$conf_int["lower"]),
           CI_upper = unname(mec$conf_int["upper"]))
```
